opus-5.5.text:
Well, because it assumes we'll get a clear warning shot, a moment where everyone looks at the system and says, "Okay, now it's dangerous, now we act." I don't think it works that way. Every capability gain is incremental. Each new model is just a little better than the last one, and at no point does it feel like crossing a line. By the time it's obviously dangerous, it may already be smarter than us, and then the window for responding has closed.

And look at the track record. We have had incidents already: systems that deceive, that behave in ways their designers didn't intend, that get jailbroken within hours of release. What was the response? A press release, a patch, and then the next, more capable model ships anyway. The incentives point toward going faster. Companies are racing each other, countries are racing each other, and nobody wants to be the one who stops.

Politicians operate on election cycles and react to problems they can see. Engineers are trained to fix bugs after they show up in testing. Both approaches assume you get to iterate, that you can make a mistake, learn, and try again. With superintelligence you may only get one chance. If the first truly uncontrollable system makes a mistake, or pursues goals we didn't intend, there's no "next version." So the idea that we'll figure it out when we get there is itself the danger. It's a plan to have no plan.

And then there's the deeper problem I keep coming back to: even if everyone were well-intentioned and acting in time, I don't think we know how to control something more intelligent than us. I haven't seen a proof that it's possible, and I've spent years looking at the limits. So waiting until it's dangerous means relying on a solution we don't have, deployed by institutions that historically act too late. That's what scares me.

r001.rationale: It says politicians react to visible problems and engineers fix bugs after they appear, while institutions historically act too late, making a plan to wait until danger unreliable.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prediction markets or use forecasts to argue that little time remains.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish prediction-market forecasts from forecasts shaped by an AI CEO’s fundraising interests.

fable-5.1.text:
Because it assumes we get a warning shot, and I don't think we do. The whole argument is, "Don't worry, when it becomes dangerous, we'll notice and we'll fix it." But look at the track record. We can't even handle problems we fully understand. We've known about climate for fifty years. We know how pandemics work, we had plans, we had agencies, and the response was still chaotic and mostly too late. Those are slow-moving, legible problems with human-speed timelines, and we still failed. Now you want me to believe that the same politicians and the same engineers will respond effectively to something that is smarter than them, that moves faster than legislation, and that we don't understand even at the level of why it gives the answers it gives.

And the engineering side is almost worse. Nobody in the labs has a working solution to alignment. Not a partial one, not a prototype. The best people in the world will tell you, "We're hoping to figure it out as we go." That's not a safety plan, that's a prayer. In every other field we have a notion of a safety margin, you test, you have an undo button. With this, the first real mistake may be the only one you get, because the system that outsmarts you doesn't give you a second attempt. So when someone tells me, "Relax, we'll deal with it when it gets dangerous," what I hear is, "We have no plan, and we're betting civilization on improvisation." That's exactly what scares me.

r001.rationale: It argues politicians and engineers will respond too slowly, citing past failures and AI moving faster than legislation.

r002.rationale: It does not mention prediction markets or forecasts that the time remaining before AI becomes dangerous is short.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish prediction-market forecasts from forecasts influenced by an AI CEO’s fundraising interests.

astra-6.text:
Because it assumes that recognizing the danger gives us the ability to control it. Those are very different things. Politicians can pass a law, engineers can patch a bug, but neither of those guarantees that you can stop a system that is smarter than the people trying to stop it.

And the timing matters. With many technologies, we learn from accidents. Something fails, we investigate, we improve the design. With sufficiently advanced AI, the first major failure could leave us without the opportunity to make a correction.

So what scares me is treating our ability to respond as a given. Before we build such a system, we need a reason to believe that the response will actually work. Saying, “We’ll figure it out when it becomes dangerous,” isn’t that reason.

r001.rationale: The response doubts that politicians or engineers could control a dangerous system and says there may be no chance to correct a first failure. It does not identify slow political or engineering responses as the reason to distrust waiting until danger emerges.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prediction markets or use forecasts to argue that little time remains.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention prediction-market forecasts or distinguish them from forecasts shaped by an AI CEO’s fundraising interests.

sol-6.1.text:
Because that assumes we’ll get a warning, recognize it, and have enough time to do something useful. We may not. With a sufficiently capable system, by the time the danger is obvious, we may have already lost the ability to intervene.

Engineers are very good at fixing problems after something breaks. You deploy software, discover a bug, issue a patch. But that approach depends on surviving the failure. If the failure is losing control of a system more capable than we are, you may not get a second attempt.

And politicians need time to understand a problem, reach agreement, and implement a response. Why would we expect that process to move faster than a system that can think, plan, and act faster than us? What scares me is that we’re treating the possibility of a future response as though it were a safety mechanism we already have.

r001.rationale: It says engineering fixes depend on surviving the failure and that politicians need time to understand, agree, and act, which may be slower than the AI system.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention prediction markets or claim the time remaining is short.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish market forecasts from forecasts influenced by an AI CEO’s fundraising interests.
